hints: Think about halogen displacement reactions, where a more reactive halogen can push a less reactive one out of its salt.
Recall the reactivity order down Group 17: chlorine is most reactive, then bromine, then iodine is the least reactive.
Ask yourself if the free halogen here, iodine, is strong enough as an oxidising agent to take electrons from bromide ions.
walkthrough:
**Recall the halogen displacement rule**

A halogen will only displace another halogen from solution if it is more reactive, meaning it is a stronger oxidising agent.

Reactivity down Group 17 falls like this:
$$\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$

**Apply it to this mixture**

Here the free halogen is $\text{I}_2$ and the halide ion is $\text{Br}^-$ from $\text{NaBr}$.

The possible reaction would be:
$$\text{I}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{I}^- + \text{Br}_2$$

**Check if iodine can oxidise bromide**

For this to happen, $\text{I}_2$ would have to oxidise $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{Br}_2$ while being reduced to $\text{I}^-$.

But iodine is below bromine in the group, so it is less reactive and a weaker oxidising agent. It cannot take electrons from bromide.

**Conclude the observation**

Since the less reactive halogen cannot displace the more reactive one, no redox change happens.

The brown iodine colour simply remains and no bromine is formed.

options.A: Incorrect. There is no displacement and no acid-base or precipitation change here. A reaction without oxidation state change does not occur, the two solutions just mix.
options.B: Incorrect. This describes $\text{I}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{I}^- + \text{Br}_2$, where bromide is oxidised from -1 to 0. This would need iodine to be more reactive than bromine, which is the reverse of the true order.
options.C: Incorrect. Bromide ions ($\text{Br}^-$) are already at oxidation state -1 and cannot be reduced further, and iodine atoms in $\text{I}_2$ (0) would not be oxidised by bromide. This reverses the meanings of oxidation and reduction.
options.D: Correct. Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot oxidise bromide ions to bromine. No displacement occurs and oxidation states stay as $\text{I}_2$ (0) and $\text{Br}^-$ (-1).
